Revised assessment: The statement is clearly hawkish—raising the federal funds rate to 3–3.25%, signaling “ongoing increases,” and continuing balance-sheet reduction—while stressing elevated inflation and war-related supply shocks. In the literature, this maps to a contractionary monetary policy shock that tends to slow activity in the near term (Romer and Romer), and it is broadly consistent with rule-based responses when inflation is above target (Taylor rule). Given elevated right-tail “inflation-at-risk” from pandemic and geopolitical shocks (Mixing it up: Inflation at risk, 2024), a strong commitment and clear operating stance help preserve credibility and anchor expectations (Goodfriend, 2002). While pandemic-era composition effects (COVID-19 Inflation Weighting in Israel, 2022) suggest some measured inflation may be transitory, the Fed’s emphasis on persistence and continued QT underscores a negative near-term growth impulse. Higher rates can also compress markups and profits (The Beginning of the Trend: Interest Rates, Profits, and Markups, 2023), aiding disinflation but reinforcing the cautious tone. Distinguishing price-level shocks from monetary inflation (On the Nature of Monetary and Price Inflation and Hyperinflation, 2021) supports tightening to avoid de-anchoring. Net tone: moderately negative for growth, supportive for long-run price stability.
